title: Now I see (John 9:13–41)
hook: the healed man is questioned, thrown out, and found again by Jesus

segments.voice: Yesterday, mud and spit, a walk to the pool called Siloam, which means Sent, and a man who came back seeing. Your line was neither sinned. Did you skip the blame and find the work? Day six hundred eighteen.

A miracle ought to end in a party. A man blind from birth can see. His neighbors should be throwing a feast. Instead, chapter nine becomes a courtroom drama. The neighbors argue about whether it's even him. Some say yes. Others say no, he just looks like him. And the man keeps saying, over and over, I am he. Then he's brought to the religious leaders, and the questions start. How did this happen? Who did it? Was it the sabbath? The man who was blind is about to be questioned three times, and he gets braver each time.

The first time, he just tells the facts: he put clay on my eyes, I washed, and I see. The leaders are divided. Some say a man who heals on the sabbath can't be from God. Others say, how can a sinner do such signs? They ask the healed man what he thinks. He says: he's a prophet. Then they call his parents. And his parents, frightened, say only: yes, this is our son, and yes, he was born blind. How he sees, we don't know. Ask him. He's of age. John says they were afraid of being put out of the synagogue. Some readers think this detail also reflects John's own time, when followers of Jesus and other Jewish communities were painfully parting ways. So the man is called back a second time, and pressed: we know this man is a sinner. And he answers: "whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." He doesn't win the theology argument. He doesn't try. He stands on the one thing he's sure of. Then he even gets cheeky: why do you want to hear it again? Will ye also be his disciples? And they throw him out. Here's the turn. "Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him," he asks: do you believe in the Son of man? Who is he, Lord? You've seen him. He's talking with you. And the man says, "Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him." Thrown out by one door, he's found by the one who came looking.
screen: then, large: `WHEREAS I WAS BLIND, NOW I SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by your one sure thing. Settle, and breathe. Think about the big questions you can't answer. About God, about suffering, about what happens next. Let them be there, unresolved. Now look for one thing you know from your own life. Something you've seen with your own eyes. A time you were helped. A change in you. A moment of beauty you can't explain away. Hold it simply, without arguing for it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let it be solid ground. The bell holds the time.
Synagogue. What the healed man's parents feared being cast out of, for saying too much about who healed him.
Your line: one thing I know. Today, when someone asks how you are or what you believe, tell one thing you know firsthand, simply, without a speech. Day six hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Christians often share testimonies, simple accounts of what God has done in their lives, and the healed man's "one thing I know" is a common model; the hymn Amazing Grace echoes his words.

original.note: Greek: I see. The healed man's last word in his famous answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a happy ending to a healing story.
what it means: the healed man is questioned, abandoned by his parents and thrown out, but grows braver, and Jesus finds him.
what a scholar hears: fear of being "put out of the synagogue" may also reflect the painful parting of ways in John's own community, later on.

notes: The 'put out of the synagogue' detail (9:22) as reflecting John's later community: associated with J. Louis Martyn and widely discussed, also debated. Presented as 'many scholars think'. Confirm.
'Amazing Grace' (John Newton, 1779; public domain) line 'was blind, but now I see'. Confirm.
Counting the man's interrogations: neighbors (9:8–12), leaders (9:13–17), leaders again (9:24–34). Script says 'questioned three times'. Confirm.
Some manuscripts lack 9:38–39a; not raised in the script.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'many scholars think' (now 'some readers'), 'decades later', the superlative 'one of the great answers in the Bible', and the hook's 'you'd think'.
